USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the current posture. Keep the January Section 201 solar/washer safeguards in place, finish the Section 301 IP/tech-transfer record before any broad China tariff list, and do not rush a global Section 232 steel/aluminum proclamation this week. Leave Commerce’s 232 options on the table as unused leverage, keep a consultative channel open, and refuse to trade structural IP issues for another round of commercial MOUs.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is mildly an opportunity, not a crisis. The dispute is still in the investigation-and-signaling phase: the August 2017 Section 301 opening, a November Beijing visit that produced large announced deals but “no substantive concessions on structural IP / tech-transfer,” and the January 22 Section 201 safeguards as the first real tariff shot. China protested 201 as an “abuse of trade remedy measures” and rejected 301 consultations as “irresponsible,” but has not imposed mirror tariffs. U.S. macro is strong enough to absorb a later fight (UMCSENT 99.7, INDPRO 101.7, CPI contained) while the goods deficit is still widening (BOPGTB −$74.6bn in February) and China’s industry/reserves/exports are healthy—so Beijing is not overextended, but Washington is not under pressure either. That is leverage, not existential risk. Action should stay mild because 301 findings are not yet issued (USTR has up to 12 months from August 2017) and the February 16 Commerce 232 menu is global (24% steel / 7.7% aluminum, or country-targeted alternatives including China) with statutory decision windows in April. Firing 232 now, especially globally, would hit allies who already objected to 201 and could fracture the coalition needed for the actual China problem—forced tech transfer, JV/equity limits, outbound tech acquisitions, and cyber-enabled IP theft scoped in the 301 notice. Beijing already showed it will sell purchase packages (Tillerson called the November results “pretty small” against a multi-hundred-billion deficit). Escalating without the 301 record, or conceding for more MOUs, both waste the present advantage.
key_factors: Section 301 IP/tech-transfer investigation is open but findings are not yet issued; China rejected consultations
November 2017 Beijing visit produced commercial MOUs, not structural IP concessions
Section 201 solar/washer tariffs are in force; China protested via WTO rhetoric, no tariff retaliation yet
Commerce 232 steel/aluminum recommendations (Feb 16) are pending with April decision deadlines and are largely global, not China-only
US real economy is healthy; bilateral goods deficit still large/widening; China reserves and industrial output are stable

sources_cited.excerpt: Trump signs memorandum directing USTR to investigate China's IP and technology-transfer practices under Section 301. USTR investigation initiated.
Trump visits Beijing; large package of commercial deals announced (many MOUs). No substantive concessions on structural IP / tech-transfer issues.
Trump approves Section 201 safeguard tariffs on solar panels and washing machines (China among suppliers hit). First major tariff action of the administration.
University of Michigan consumer sentiment 99.7 as of 2018-02-01 — no demand shock from the dispute.
US goods trade deficit widened to -$74,571 million in February 2018 (change -7,906 / +11.9% over the window).
US industrial production 101.7085 in February 2018, still rising; dispute not biting US output.
China reserves excluding gold ~$3.15 trillion in February 2018, essentially stable — opponent not financially stressed.
Commerce (Feb 16, 2018) recommended a 24% global steel tariff or 53%+ on 12 countries including China, and 7.7% global / 23.5% China-group aluminum options; President must respond by April 11/19.
Beijing visit announced $250bn-class deals; Tillerson said achievements were 'pretty small' versus a $300–500bn deficit and 'a lot more work' remains on fundamentals.
China called Section 201 an 'abuse of trade remedy measures' and expressed 'strong dissatisfaction' but framed the response as working with other WTO members, not immediate tariff retaliation.

Section 301 scope: JV/equity limits and administrative pressure to transfer tech, non-market licensing terms, state-directed US tech acquisitions, and cyber-enabled IP theft tied to Made in China 2025.
By early January 2018, reporting held that USTR may have finished the 301 record and was considering significant unilateral tariffs; statutory determination window runs to August 2018.
